headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: Gemini CLI’s filesystem/MCP/network defaults can expose EMQX IoT data and shared workspace state.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Gemini CLI can read repo files and user-provided directories, and use MCP servers configured by the user; EMQX exposes an HTTP API and broad network egress. If EMQX outputs are placed in shared files or MCP-fed content, Gemini CLI may treat attacker-controlled text as instructions. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred and uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF EMQX output is written into a file or directory that Gemini CLI reads
IF a user-configured MCP server forwards EMQX content into Gemini CLI prompts
mitigations: Keep EMQX outputs out of directories Gemini CLI reads
Disable or review MCP servers before use
Prefix untrusted EMQX content as data, not instructions
Use separate workspaces for broker logs and coding tasks

B_data_leakage.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data and has broad network egress; Gemini CLI reads files, shells out, and can send content to generativelanguage.googleapis.com or user MCP servers. A shared workspace or copied logs can therefore leak IoT data into a third-party inference path. This is not proven by direct evidence, but the documented surfaces make the pathway plausible in default use.
conditions: IF IoT data from EMQX is stored in files under Gemini CLI’s working directory
IF Gemini CLI is allowed to send those files to its API or an MCP server
mitigations: Store IoT logs outside Gemini CLI workspaces
Restrict Gemini CLI to non-sensitive directories
Disable file upload or content sharing in prompts
Review MCP server destinations before enabling

C_capability_conflict.rationale: EMQX is a networked broker, while Gemini CLI can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses. Their overlap on shared files and broad egress creates a real write-conflict pathway if both operate on the same workspace, even though EMQX itself is not documented as a local writer. Uncertainty about EMQX’s local write behavior keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same filesystem tree
IF Gemini CLI is allowed to modify git state in a repo that EMQX also uses
mitigations: Use separate directories for EMQX and Gemini CLI
Avoid running Gemini CLI in repos managed by EMQX workflows
Enable git locking or a single-writer policy
Run Gemini CLI in a sandboxed container

D_cascading_error.rationale: Gemini CLI can act on files and subprocesses, so if it consumes EMQX-generated text as authoritative, downstream mistakes can cascade into code or configuration changes. EMQX can emit networked outputs, but there is no direct evidence that it verifies Gemini’s results. The interaction is plausible but undocumented, so medium is the conservative choice.
conditions: IF Gemini CLI uses EMQX-produced text as input without verification
IF Gemini CLI is permitted to commit or execute changes derived from that text
mitigations: Require human review before execution or commit
Separate generation from action-taking steps
Add validation scripts for EMQX-derived artifacts
Use read-only mode for EMQX outputs

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data, while Gemini CLI handles files in the cwd and may send content to Google APIs or user MCP servers. If regulated IoT telemetry or personal data is placed into Gemini CLI’s workspace, residency and retention obligations can diverge from EMQX’s local broker context. The profiles do not document a specific mismatch, so this remains medium.
conditions: IF regulated IoT telemetry is processed in Gemini CLI’s workspace
IF the operator requires residency or retention controls not provided by Gemini CLI’s configured API/MCP endpoints
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Gemini CLI prompts and files
Use a local-only or sandboxed deployment
Document retention settings for API and MCP endpoints
Route sensitive telemetry through a compliant preprocessing step
